response:
Early-exit architectures let a model halt computation at intermediate layers when a confidence signal — typically softmax entropy or a learned halting score — crosses a threshold, trading accuracy for speed. The central question is whether the internal representations at the layer where a given input exits are semantically coherent with the representations that would have formed at the final layer — and whether the answer changes systematically as the halting threshold is tuned. The key concepts in tension are: (1) representation drift, the progressive transformation of token embeddings across depth that is not monotonically refinement but involves destructive reorganization; (2) adaptive halting thresholds, which create a non-uniform depth distribution across a batch, meaning different inputs see different amounts of this drift; and (3) the exit classifier's calibration surface, which is trained on a fixed depth but must generalize across depths. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the correlation structure between which inputs exit early and which inputs are hardest — easy inputs exit early not because they need less computation, but because the model becomes confident early, and the representation at that early layer may be geometrically distant from the final-layer manifold in ways that make downstream tasks (retrieval, generation, classification heads) quietly degrade without any signal from the confidence metric itself. The beginner sees a speed-accuracy tradeoff; the expert sees a potential distribution shift internal to the model that the halting criterion is blind to.

Downstream task heads — whether classification probes, retrieval encoders, or generation prefixes — are trained on representations from a fixed depth, typically the final layer, and implicitly assume that the embedding manifold has a specific curvature, density, and linear separability profile. When early-exiting inputs land at shallower layers, their representations occupy a geometrically distinct region: work by Geva et al. (2022) on transformer feed-forward layers shows that middle layers perform significant "promotion" operations that move token representations toward final vocabulary/semantic targets, meaning shallow exits catch embeddings mid-promotion. In systems like DeeBERT (Xin et al., 2020) and CALM (Schuster et al., 2022), shared classification heads are placed at each exit point and fine-tuned jointly, which partially compensates — but the compensation is local; the head learns the geometry at that layer for training examples that happened to exit there, not for the full input distribution. The danger is a systematic mismatch: inputs that are "easy" by the halting criterion (low entropy early) may be easy precisely because they activate shallow, high-frequency features — proper nouns, common collocations — whose representations haven't undergone the depth-dependent anisotropy compression that Ethayarajh (2019) documented in BERT, where upper layers become far more anisotropic and thus more linearly separable for semantic tasks. A shared head trained predominantly on final-layer geometry will therefore see early-exit embeddings as poorly conditioned inputs — compressed into a different region of the cone — and may produce confidently wrong outputs with no calibration signal. The practical implication is that the embedding space is not a single coherent geometry but a layered stack of partially incompatible manifolds, and any head that spans multiple exit depths is implicitly doing cross-manifold generalization, which is rarely explicitly evaluated.

The evidence suggests dip position scales predictably with model depth but not linearly — in BERT-base (12 layers) the representational transition zone identified by Tenney et al. (2019) through edge probing sits roughly at layers 5-7, while in BERT-large (24 layers) the analogous zone shifts to layers 9-14, implying the transition occupies approximately 40-50% of total depth regardless of absolute size, which would make dip position a roughly fixed fractional depth phenomenon. Training data distribution shifts the dip more dramatically than model size does: models trained on syntactically homogeneous corpora (e.g., filtered web text) show narrower dips because fewer competing feature systems need reconciliation, while models trained on heterogeneous mixtures — code, math, natural language interleaved, as in the Pile — show wider, shallower dips because the reorganization must serve more divergent representational demands simultaneously, a pattern consistent with Raghu et al.'s (2017) SVCCA findings on width of representational transition zones in vision models under distribution shift. The dip width is particularly telling: a narrow dip (1-2 layers) suggests a sharp phase transition where a dominant feature system rapidly displaces another, while a wide dip (4-6 layers) suggests overlapping, competitive reorganization — the latter is what you'd expect from models with high intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, which Ansuini et al. (2019) measured in ResNets and found correlated with generalization difficulty of the training distribution. Using dip geometry as a probe for critical computational transitions is genuinely promising: if you map dip position and width across a suite of tasks and find that the dip for syntactic tasks occurs 2-3 layers shallower than for semantic tasks on the same model, you've identified a layered processing schedule that tells you where to place task-specific adapters or early exits without ablation studies. The most operationally useful finding would be if dip geometry is input-class-specific rather than model-global — meaning different input subpopulations have their own reorganization windows — which would imply that a single fixed early-exit threshold is structurally incapable of avoiding the dip for all inputs simultaneously, and adaptive per-class thresholds are not just an optimization but a architectural necessity.

The error types are systematically different and the distinction is mechanistically interpretable: exits before the reorganization window produce errors that resemble surface-level feature confusions — wrong outputs that are phonologically similar, syntactically parallel, or domain-adjacent to the correct answer, because the representation still encodes shallow distributional features without semantic disambiguation; exits inside the dip produce a more pathological error type where the model outputs high-confidence garbage — predictions that are neither shallow-feature-similar nor semantically related — because the representation is in a partially destructured state where early features have been suppressed but late features haven't activated, leaving the embedding in a low-density, geometrically anomalous region the exit head has never been trained on. This distinction maps onto what Huang et al. (2017) observed in multi-scale dense networks: premature exits produced label-smoothed errors clustered near decision boundaries, while mid-reorganization exits produced outlier errors far from any training cluster, measurable as elevated Mahalanobis distance from the head's training distribution. That geometric signature — specifically, anomalously high Mahalanobis distance or low-density placement in the exit head's feature space — is exactly what a lightweight online detector could exploit: you compute a running covariance estimate per exit head during training, then at inference flag any exit where the representation's Mahalanobis distance exceeds a calibrated percentile threshold, which adds roughly O(d²) memory per exit head and a single matrix multiply per inference step, negligible compared to attention costs. Lee et al. (2018) demonstrated this approach for out-of-distribution detection in standard classifiers with AUROC above 0.9 on CIFAR/SVHN, and the early-exit case is structurally identical — the "out-of-distribution" inputs are those whose reorganization window hasn't closed yet, making them geometrically anomalous to the exit head even when the halting criterion fires confidently. The critical implementation detail is that the detector must be calibrated per exit layer using only the inputs that naturally reached that layer during training, not the full training set — otherwise the covariance estimate is contaminated by representations from inputs with different reorganization schedules, which would inflate variance and reduce detection sensitivity precisely for the mid-dip cases you most need to catch.
